transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-08
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~63 minutes
Attendees: Samir Khan (Redwood AE), Elena Park (Redwood SE), Jared Liu (Vertex ML Eng), Priya Nair (Vertex Platform), Marco Ruiz (Vertex CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, might be noisy):
- Deep dive on architecture-specific tuning across Llama / Mistral / Qwen; focus on MoE routing overheads, RoPE scaling issues at long context, KV cache and batching strategies, and VPC/on-prem constraints.
- Agreed next steps: share benchmarks, run PoC in customer's VPC, gather request distribution.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone, uh thanks for carving out time, we wanted to do a technical deep dive on model-specific tuning. elena and i will walk through runtime considerations for llama, mistral, qwen, plus moe routing and rope scaling.
[00:22] Marco: nice, thanks. short ask from our side — we need to understand perf/cost tradeoffs for our live assistant, and the constraints for running in our VPC.
[00:35] Elena: great — quick housekeeping, i'll note that some terms might be slightly off in the transcript, like RoPE sometimes appears as rook in the notes, and qwen might be transcribed as q-win.
[00:48] Jared: ha okay that's fine. we have fairly spiky traffic, 90th percentile seq len ~512 but long tail to 8k, maybe 10k.
[01:05] Priya: and our security team requires KMS integration, SAML SSO, audit logs and no egress without approval.
[01:12] Samir: understood. on the VPC/on-prem front — Redwood's private deploy supports customer-managed control plane and KMS/HSM integrations, and we can run the inference plane in your subnet. we'll share the VPC-deploy doc after.
[01:32] Elena: jumping into the model tuning side — let's start with Llama family. primary levers there are: quantization level (fp16 / int8 / q4 variants), batch sizing, KV cache placement, and attention optimizations. with Llama-2-13B we see good latency/cost tradeoff using Q4_0 for many workloads but watch for generation quality degradation on some prompts.
[01:58] Jared: for quality-sensitive flows (we rerank and then call out to a higher-precision model), so we care about that trade-off.
[02:10] Elena: right, a pattern we recommend is hybrid: use a cheaper quantized model for first-pass and route to fp16/dedicated variant for critical outputs. also prefix caching helps if many requests share a common context.
[02:28] Marco: can you explain prefix caching — is that KV cache not persisted across requests?
[02:36] Samir: good q — prefix/KV caching can be persisted for a session or per-user to avoid recomputing attention keys for the same prefix. on Redwood runtime we store compressed KV shards in GPU memory or local NVMe, and warm them when requests hit. there is a trade: persisting many sessions increases memory pressure on KV cache.
[02:58] Elena: and that ties to batching — continuous batching helps throughput but may increase tail latency. we tune the batch scheduler per-route: latency SLOs for real-time chat vs throughput for async tasks.
[03:18] Jared: how do you handle the long-tail sequence lengths — our 8k-10k requests will blow up KV memory.
[03:27] Elena: for long context we recommend adaptive truncation and dynamic sharding of KV across GPUs, plus RoPE scaling where applicable. which brings us to RoPE.
[03:39] Marco: yes RoPE scaling — we've seen drift when moving to longer contexts. any concrete techniques?
[03:46] Elena: RoPE (rotary positional embeddings) scaling can be handled two ways — static rescaling and linear scaling factors applied at inference time. for some models (qwen in particular) naive scaling leads to degraded semantics; we use calibrated scaling factors and sometimes rescale attention matrices during compilation. note: transcripts might call it rook scaling in some notes.
[04:10] Samir: also important: if you use a checkpoint that was pretrained with a particular RoPE frequency, changing it will require careful evals; we often run a small held-out prompt suite to check for hallucination/regression after scaling.
[04:28] Jared: does Redwood support automatic rope-rescaling per model?
[04:33] Elena: yes, for a curated subset of models (Llama variants, Mistral, Qwen) we have model-specific rescale profiles. we'll share the profiles in the benchmark sheet.
[04:44] Marco: ok. next, MoE — we are considering an MoE hybrid to reduce FLOPs, but worried about routing overhead and tail latency.
[04:55] Samir: MoE introduces two major runtime costs: per-token expert selection (gating compute) and load imbalance across experts leading to less parallel efficiency. the gating step is cheap relative to a full FFN, but the fragmentation of requests to experts can raise latency.
[05:16] Elena: and the routing network may need extra memory and synchrony if using top-k gating; there's also increased network traffic in multi-GPU setups. on Redwood we support capped-routing: we limit active experts per batch and fall back to a dense FFN when imbalance occurs. that reduces worst-case tail latency at the cost of some compute efficiency.
[05:40] Jared: so would MoE save us money for our workload? we have many short sessions with varied prompts.
[05:48] Elena: MoE tends to shine with large batch sizes and homogeneous workloads where expert specialization helps. for spiky, short-chat workloads you might not realize the theoretical FLOP reduction because routing overhead and small batch sizes dominate. we'd likely recommend a dense optimized variant for your profile unless you run larger batched inference (e.g., async hits for offline summarization).
[06:10] Priya: what about quantization interacting with MoE? any constraints?
[06:16] Elena: quantization of expert FFNs is feasible, but gating itself is sensitive — using low-precision for gating can introduce misrouting. typical approach: keep gating in fp16 and quantize expert weights to Q4_x. that retains routing fidelity while saving memory.
[06:33] Marco: you mentioned fallback to dense — is that seamless or needs model changes?
[06:37] Samir: seamless in the runtime — we maintain dense variants of important models or emulate MoE by mapping to a dense FFN when needed. customers can pin the fallback policy.
[06:47] Jared: latency numbers — do you have ballpark 95/99th for Llama 13B fp16 vs q4?
[06:56] Elena: our internal baseline on a 80GB A10 / H100 class node (single-stream inference): Llama-13B fp16 95th around 120-180ms for short prompts (<=512), q4_0 95th ~95-140ms; 99th increases substantially with context and depends on batching. i'll include concrete numbers in the spreadsheet — these are ballparks.
[07:22] Samir: keep in mind we can also use model variants with attention optimizations for long context (memory-optimized kernels) which shift the curves.
[07:33] Priya: what's the smallest quantized variant you'd recommend for safety-critical outputs?
[07:37] Elena: for safety/QA you probably want fp16 or Q4_1 with revist evals. Q4_0 is aggressive but often fine for first-pass. Q5/Q6 experimental schemes are still risky for accuracy in many tasks.
[07:52] Marco: can you speak to kernel selection and compilation — e.g., when Redwood picks fused attention or attention-slicing?
[07:59] Elena: the compiler chooses kernels based on model architecture, seq length distribution and hardware. for short seqs we favor fused kernels with lower overhead; for long contexts we switch to split-attention kernels that reduce memory spikes. that selection happens during model warm-up and can be tuned per-route.
[08:20] Jared: ok good. on VPC/on-prem we have network isolation and limited outbound egress. how do you handle model downloads and updates?
[08:28] Samir: for private deploys we support preloaded images and offline model staging. models can be loaded via customer-approved registry or via secure transfer into their subnet. updates are scheduled with maintenance windows and we provide hashes and signatures for verification.
[08:43] Priya: and logging — we need audit logs and token-level cost breakdowns anonymized. is that available?
[08:50] Samir: yes, Redwood Console supports per-token cost breakdowns, route-level tracing and audit logs; in private deployments those logs can be forwarded to your SIEM. there is also an option to redact sensitive fields before export.
[09:05] Elena: back to batching and KV cache — a practical tip: set a warm-up policy for sessions that are likely to be reused (e.g., 30-60s retention) and cap total persisted sessions. also measure memory pressure and evict least-recently-used session caches.
[09:22] Jared: any numbers on how much KV saving you get with prefix caching?
[09:26] Elena: depends on reuse rate; with 30% session reuse we saw effective per-token compute drop by ~20-30% on some corpora, because you avoid recomputing the encoder keys. but memory overhead increases correspondingly.
[09:44] Marco: questions on RoPE again — our pretraining data used relative position encodings, will that complicate things?
[09:50] Elena: relative pos encodings and RoPE are related — many models use RoPE-style relative encodings. the key is to align inference scaling with the model's training regimen. if they differ, you'll see degradation in tasks sensitive to absolute positions. we usually run a small eval harness with a handful of positional-sensitive prompts.
[10:12] Jared: you mentioned quantized kernels — does Redwood do kernel-level optimization for Q4 kernels?
[10:18] Elena: yes — we have optimized kernels for common quant formats; some are vendor-specific (NVIDIA TensorRT / cuBLAS fused ops) and some are our own CPU/GPU fused primitives. performance varies by GPU generation.
[10:32] Samir: also, for Qwen specifically, note that Qwen models sometimes have unusual layernorm ordering and require specific compilation passes; we've seen naive quantization break normalization behavior.
[10:46] Jared: can you give an example of a broken behavior?
[10:49] Elena: for example, folding layernorm into linear ops without recalibration can shift activations and amplify hallucinations. we run calibration on a small dataset to mitigate.
[11:02] Marco: are there tooling hooks to validate a new quantized model before rolling to prod?
[11:07] Samir: yes — Redwood Optimize has a validation harness: automatic evals on your prompt set, quality regressions alerts, and staged rollouts (canary -> 50% -> full) with automatic fallback if quality drops.
[11:22] Priya: good. on the security checklist — SOC2, ISO? we need compliance docs.
[11:27] Samir: we will share SOC 2 Type II and ISO attestation docs in the security packet. for private deploys we also provide network diagrams and configuration templates.
[11:38] Jared: back to MoE load balancing — you mentioned capped-routing and fallbacks. how do you determine thresholds?
[11:46] Elena: thresholds are configured based on observed expert load and latency SLOs; typical threshold: if >20% of requests experience >2x latency of median due to imbalance, we enable fallback for that route. thresholds are tunable per-customer.
[12:04] Marco: do you have metrics we can monitor to detect routing hot spots?
[12:09] Elena: yes — expert utilization histograms, gating entropy, per-expert latency and queue length. those are surfaced in the Console.
[12:18] Jared: great. any network considerations for MoE in a multi-node VPC?
[12:23] Elena: MoE can require cross-node all-to-all for expert outputs if experts are sharded — that increases network egress and latency. we prefer colocating experts on the same node when possible, or using partitioning strategies that minimize cross-node traffic.
[12:40] Samir: practical recommendation: for VPC-based dedicated pools, allocate fewer nodes and larger memory per node to co-locate experts, rather than lots of small nodes. that reduces egress and improves tail latency.
[12:53] Priya: that affects our capacity planning. can you provide a sample capacity estimate?
[12:58] Elena: we'll include a sample in the benchmark sheet — high level: for your peak QPS and 95th latency target, we'll model GPU count under fp16, q4_0, and MoE scenarios and show cost per million tokens.
[13:15] Jared: about rope again — does tokenization or position interpolations affect it? for example we sometimes re-tokenize preprompt.
[13:23] Elena: tokenization doesn't change RoPE math, but prompt engineering that alters positions (e.g., adding big system prompts) can shift positions and push tokens to higher indices. that's when rope scaling or truncation matters.
[13:37] Marco: any pitfalls for on-prem hardware — customers often use older GPUs.
[13:42] Elena: older GPUs may not support newer fused kernels or int8 kernels; we then fall back to less optimized paths and see throughput reductions. for on-prem, we recommend testing with the exact GPU generation. Redwood can provide a compatibility matrix.
[13:56] Samir: also consider NVMe spill to reduce OOMs for KV cache on long-context models. that trades I/O for memory and increases latency but keeps service available.
[14:09] Jared: how do you decide between on-GPU KV and NVMe spill?
[14:13] Elena: it's dynamic: monitor GPU memory pressure and latency SLOs; if memory pressure causes OOMs, enabling NVMe spill with prefetching reduces failures. we tune prefetch to hide I/O latency.
[14:27] Priya: about observability — can we get token-level traces for debugging a production incident?
[14:33] Samir: yes, with redaction and sample policies. we recommend sampling 1 in N requests to keep cost manageable.
[14:42] Elena: i'd like to show a quick architecture sketch — (screen share noise) ...
[15:00] [SCREEN SHARE break — omitted in transcript]
[18:12] Jared: nice diagram. any guidance on warm start for models when traffic spikes?
[18:18] Samir: pre-warming policy: keep a small pool of idle model instances and prefetch common prefixes; for sudden spikes, autoscaling kicks in but there's a few-second warmup. for strict 100ms SLOs you'll need reserved capacity.
[18:38] Marco: what's the cost delta for reserved capacity vs on-demand?
[18:42] Elena: reserved Dedicated pools are ~30-50% cheaper for steady loads depending on commitment. we'll include pricing examples in the spreadsheet.
[18:52] Jared: one more on quantization — do you support delta-quant or per-channel quantization?
[18:58] Elena: we support per-channel quant and some mixed-block formats; specifics vary by model and kernel. per-channel often gives better accuracy for small weights.
[19:12] Priya: what about regression alerts — can we detect when a new quantized rollout changes API-level behavior?
[19:18] Samir: yes — Redwood Optimize can run eval suites and trigger regression alerts tied to prompt sets. you can configure thresholds for metrics like exact-match, F1, or custom heuristics.
[19:33] Jared: we'll need that for safety.
[19:36] Marco: circling back to RoPE — do you support absolute/relative hybrid encodings?
[19:42] Elena: some models use hybrid; the runtime respects the model definition and we don't rewrite encoding semantics, but we provide rescaling adapters for a small set of models. those adapters are validated on held-out prompts.
[19:56] Jared: do you have examples of where rope scaling improved results at 4k+ context?
[20:02] Elena: yes — for an internal summarization task we saw coherence improve when applying calibrated rope rescale and a light retrain on position-sensitive examples. but results are model-dependent.
[20:18] Samir: ok, let's recap action items before we run out of time.
[20:24] Marco: sure.
[20:26] Samir: Samir will send the benchmark and VPC deployment doc. Elena will run PoC baseline in their VPC for Llama-13B fp16 vs q4 and also test Qwen 1B. Jared will provide seq hist and sample traces.
[20:41] Priya: timeline estimate? can we expect the first PoC numbers in ~1 week?
[20:46] Elena: yes — baseline within 5-7 business days assuming we get traces and VPC access.
[20:52] Marco: okay.
[20:54] Samir: any final q's?
[20:56] Jared: none here. thanks all.
[21:00] Samir: thanks -- we'll follow up with artifacts.
